specPoints.text: use the relationship between force, change in momentum and time taken: force = change in momentum time taken ( mv − mu ) F = t

primer.text: From the Momentum subtopic you already know how to compute momentum as mass multiplied by velocity, and from earlier in Forces & Motion you know that a resultant force changes an object's velocity. This note joins the two ideas: a resultant force acting on a moving object changes that object's momentum, and how quickly the change happens decides how large the force must be.

lessons.title: Forces & momentum
lessons.opening: Push a moving trolley and it speeds up; drag your feet on it and it slows down. Either way its momentum changes, and this lesson turns that observation into the syllabus equation: force equals change in momentum divided by time. You will also learn the symbol-by-symbol anatomy of F = (mv − mu)/t and the sign rule that keeps rebound questions honest.
keyPoints: A resultant force on a moving object changes its velocity — speeding it up or slowing it down — and so changes the object's momentum.
Combining F = ma with p = mv gives F = (mv − mu)/t: force equals change in momentum divided by the time taken.
In the equation, m is mass in kilograms, u the initial velocity, v the final velocity and t the time in seconds.
A momentum change is quoted in kg m/s, and the force that causes it in newtons (N).
Choose one direction as positive before substituting: motion the opposite way enters the equation as a negative value.

low.restatement: A force that speeds an object up or slows it down is changing its momentum, and the force equals that momentum change divided by the time taken.
low.analogy: Momentum is the cargo of motion in a trolley; a force is the hand loading or unloading it, and time is how long the hand gets to work.
low.examPointer: When a question names the relationship, write F = (mv − mu)/t in full — marks sit in the formula as well as in the final number.

medium.restatement: The equation is a double substitution: p = mv turned into before-and-after values (mu and mv), then fed into F = ma with a = (v − u)/t.
medium.analogy: Treat momentum like a bank balance: mu is the opening balance, mv the closing balance, and force the payment rate moving money between them during time t.
medium.examPointer: Sign discipline earns the marks: fix the initial direction as positive and carry every minus through mv − mu before you divide.

check.stem: For a moving object, a resultant force produces:

options.text: A change in the object's mass
options.explanation: Forces change motion, not the amount of matter present.
Accelerating or decelerating a moving object is precisely a momentum change.

options.text: Nothing unless a collision takes place
options.explanation: Any resultant force on a moving object changes its momentum, collision or not.

options.text: A change of direction only, never of speed
options.explanation: A force can change speed as well as direction.

check.stem: Combining F = ma with momentum p = mv over a contact time t gives:

options.explanation: The momentum terms subtract, because Δp is final minus initial.
That is the numerator alone; the division by time has been dropped.
Substituting a = (v − u)/t into F = ma and multiplying by m lands exactly here.
The contact time divides the change; multiplying is the inverse operation.

check.stem: In the force equation, the change in momentum is measured in:

options.explanation: Momentum change is mass × velocity change, so its unit is kg m/s.
Newtons measure the force itself, not the momentum change inside it.
m/s belongs to each velocity, not to mass × velocity.
Kilograms measure mass alone.

check.stem: In the force equation F = (mv − mu)/t, the letter u stands for:

options.explanation: u and v are swapped: u comes first in time.
Acceleration is a, from F = ma.
The momentum change is the whole numerator mv − mu, not one letter.
u is the initial velocity; v is the final one.

check.stem: A ball bounces straight back along its original path. Taking the outward direction as positive, its return velocity is entered as:

options.explanation: Only motion along the chosen positive direction counts positive; the return leg runs the other way.
The return motion is opposite to the chosen positive direction, so its velocity enters as negative.
A rebounding ball is still moving fast; zero would mean instant rest.

options.text: Unsigned until a direction is declared
options.explanation: A direction has been declared here, and velocity always carries a sign in this equation.

check.stem: State the equation that links force with the momentum change and the time, and give the unit of that momentum change.
check.modelAnswer: F = (mv − mu)/t, with the force in newtons and the numerator mv − mu — the momentum change — in kg m/s.

check.stem: Why must one direction be chosen as positive before velocities are substituted into the force equation?
check.modelAnswer: Velocity is a vector, so motion in the reverse direction must be substituted as a negative value; without that sign convention the momentum change, and hence the force, comes out wrong.

check.stem: Explain why a resultant force on a moving object changes its momentum.
check.modelAnswer: A resultant force changes the object's velocity — speeding it up or slowing it down. Since momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, any velocity change must also change the momentum.

check.stem: A 2 kg ball rolling at 6 m/s is brought to rest in 0.5 s. Taking its initial direction as positive, calculate the force on the ball.
check.modelAnswer: mv = 2 × 0 = 0 and mu = 2 × 6 = 12 kg m/s, so Δp = 0 − 12 = −12 kg m/s. F = Δp/t = −12 / 0.5 = −24 N: the force acts opposite to the ball's motion.

lessons.title: Rate of change in momentum
lessons.opening: A change of momentum can arrive gently or with a bang, and the only difference is time. Divide the same change by a long contact time and the force is tame; divide it by a blink and the force is brutal. This lesson reads the equation as a rate, then follows two worked collisions — a ball on a racket and a car on a wall.
keyPoints: Force is the momentum change per second — the rate at which a body's momentum changes.
Squeezing a momentum change into a shorter time makes the force bigger.
Force and contact time are inversely proportional: doubling the time halves the force, and halving the time doubles it.
The same 0.5 kg m/s momentum change delivers 0.25 N over 2.0 s but 5.0 N over just 0.1 s.
A car rebounding from a wall carries a negative final velocity, so the calculated force comes out negative — opposite to its initial motion.

low.restatement: The same momentum change divided by a shorter time gives a bigger force — force and time pull in opposite directions.
low.analogy: Catch an egg with stiff arms and it stops instantly and splats; let your hands drift back and the longer stop softens the force.
low.examPointer: When a question doubles or halves the contact time at fixed momentum change, answer with the inverse move: halve or double the force.

medium.restatement: Force as a rate means how much momentum changes each second, not how much changes in total.
medium.analogy: A fixed momentum change is a fixed journey; contact time is the pace you travel it, and rushing the journey spikes the force.
medium.examPointer: Airbags, seatbelts and crumple zones are this law in disguise: they stretch the contact time to cut the peak force.

check.stem: If the contact time of a collision doubles while the momentum change stays fixed, the force:

options.explanation: The proportion is inverse, not direct.
The force depends on the time through the division.
Nothing in the equation squares the time.
A fixed momentum change divided by twice the time gives half the force.

check.stem: Calling force the rate of change of momentum means the force equals the:

options.text: Momentum change multiplied by the time taken
options.explanation: The time divides the change; multiplying is the inverse operation.

options.text: Momentum change on its own, time ignored
options.explanation: A rate always carries a per-time element.

options.text: Momentum change divided by the time taken
options.explanation: Force is how much momentum changes per second of contact.

options.text: Velocity change divided by the object's mass
options.explanation: That mixes unrelated quantities; mass multiplies, it does not divide here.

check.stem: A racket changes a ball's momentum by 0.5 kg m/s during a 0.1 s hit. The force on the ball is:

options.explanation: That multiplies 0.5 by 0.1 instead of dividing.
That is the force for a 2.0 s contact, not this 0.1 s hit.
That flips the division and computes 0.1 / 0.5.

check.stem: A 1000 kg car hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds along its original path at 2 m/s after 2 s of contact. Taking the initial direction as positive, the average force on the car is:

options.explanation: It treats the rebound as +2 m/s, giving (2000 − 10000)/2.
Same size but the minus sign was dropped; the force opposes the initial motion.
That divides only the initial momentum (10000 / 2), losing the final-momentum term.

check.stem: The exam phrase 'inversely proportional' means that when the time for a momentum change shrinks by a factor of 4, the force:

options.explanation: The two quantities move in opposite directions.
A proportional link always responds to the change.
Nothing squares the factor here.
Divide the time by 4 and the force multiplies by 4.

check.stem: Define force as a rate of change.
check.modelAnswer: Force is the momentum change per second: the change in momentum divided by the time over which it happens.

check.stem: State what happens to the force when the time over which a momentum change happens gets shorter.
check.modelAnswer: The force gets bigger: with the momentum change fixed, a shorter time means dividing by less, and the two quantities are inversely proportional.

check.stem: Explain why an identical momentum change can produce very different forces in two hits.
check.modelAnswer: F = Δp/t with the momentum change fixed: dividing by a smaller time gives a larger value. Force and time are inversely proportional, so the shorter contact delivers the bigger force.

check.stem: A 0.5 kg ball strikes a wall at 8 m/s and rebounds along its original path at 2 m/s, touching the wall for 0.25 s. Taking the initial direction as positive, calculate the force on the ball.
check.modelAnswer: mv = 0.5 × (−2) = −1 kg m/s and mu = 0.5 × 8 = 4 kg m/s, so Δp = −1 − 4 = −5 kg m/s. F = Δp/t = −5 / 0.25 = −20 N: a 20 N force acting opposite to the ball's initial motion.

glossary.definition: The quantity a moving object carries because of its motion: mass multiplied by velocity, with units of kg m/s.
Final momentum minus initial momentum (mv − mu); the quantity that a force acting over a time alters.
The single overall force on an object; it appears in both F = ma and the momentum equation.
How much a quantity changes per unit time; force is the momentum change per second.
Paired so that multiplying one quantity by a factor divides the other by the same factor.
The duration for which a striking object and the surface it strikes stay in touch.

workedExample.prompt: A 1500 kg car runs into a wall while moving at 15 m/s and bounces straight back at 5 m/s; the impact lasts 3 s. Calculate the average force on the car and state which way it acts.
steps: Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is v = −5 m/s, and list the knowns: m = 1500 kg, u = 15 m/s, t = 3 s.
Write the relationship: F = (mv − mu)/t, the momentum change divided by the contact time.
Momentum after: mv = 1500 × (−5) = −7500 kg m/s; momentum before: mu = 1500 × 15 = 22500 kg m/s.
Divide by the contact time: F = −30000 / 3 = −10000 N.
workedExample.finalAnswer: F = −10000 N — a 10000 N force acting opposite to the car's original direction of travel.
